stories.headline: Iranian attack sparks fire at a Bahrain industrial site
body: Bahrain says an Iranian attack hit a civilian industrial facility and started a fire; no injuries were reported.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it targeted US forces at two bases, in al-Riffa and Awali.
Bahrain says its air defences intercepted several attacks.
stories.vc: Attacks on Gulf industry add to energy and insurance risks.

stories.headline: Drones set a Russia-linked cargo ship on fire off Finland
body: Two drones hit the Sparta II, a Kaliningrad-bound cargo ship, in the Gulf of Finland.
Finland says the ship has links to Russia's armed forces; Ukraine likely launched the drones.
The crew was evacuated as Finnish and Estonian crews fought the fire.
stories.vc: Attacks at sea raise shipping and insurance risks in the Baltic.

image.credit: Thomas Gartz from Lovisa, Finland / Wikimedia Commons

stories.statLabel: age of a man who fled his village
stories.headline: Sudan's war leaves elderly people alone in displacement camps
body: Hundreds of elderly people are living in a displacement camp in western Omdurman, Sudan.
Seventy-year-old Hamad Mohammed Adam fled after the RSF attacked his village near Bara in August.
Many older people now look after grandchildren or survive alone.
stories.vc: Aid funding has not kept pace with Sudan's needs.

stories.headline: Startup stocks miss the market rally; Paytm falls 10.8%
body: Only 22 of 69 listed new-age tech stocks rose this week, even as benchmark indices gained for a fourth week.
Paytm fell 10.8%; Zelio E-Mobility led gainers with a 19.6% rise.
Their combined value stayed near $176.9 billion.
stories.joke: The party was on Dalal Street; startups stayed home.
stories.vc: Investors are picking big, steady stocks over loss-making tech.

stories.headline: Atomberg and Voltas team up to make AC compressors in India
body: Atomberg and Tata-owned Voltas have signed a joint venture to make AC compressors in India.
Voltas will take 50% of an Atomberg subsidiary, and each side will put in up to ₹100 crore.
The deal gives IPO-bound Atomberg a big customer.
stories.joke: Cooling India, one compressor at a time.
stories.vc: Local compressor-making reduces India's reliance on imports.

stories.headline: Tax agency probes ₹1 lakh crore of China-linked gaming deals
body: GST intelligence officers searched gaming operators in Vijayawada and Hyderabad.
They are probing about ₹1 lakh crore of online gaming transactions linked to China.
They suspect money was sent to China via crypto after India banned real-money gaming.
stories.joke: The house always wins, until the taxman shows up.
stories.vc: Illegal offshore gaming drains tax revenue and hurts legal firms.

stories.headline: Unhedged: can Anthropic keep up its rocket-like start?
body: The FT's Unhedged podcast looks at Anthropic's IPO, the biggest in history.
Its shares rose 17% on day one, even as the Nasdaq 100 fell 2.2%.
Rob Armstrong asks whether the AI lab can sustain the rise.
stories.joke: Gravity is a bear market concept.
stories.vc: Anthropic is now a test case for whether AI valuations hold up.

stories.headline: Startup sues Apple in India over its NameDrop feature
body: US startup GG Technologies is suing Apple in India, claiming NameDrop copies its patented contact-sharing tech.
It wants about ₹1,500 crore ($162 million) in damages and an injunction.
It filed in October after mediation failed. (Axios Pro Rata had nothing checkable, so this is TechCrunch's report.)
stories.vc: India's courts are becoming a venue for global patent fights.

stories.headline: Microdrama startup Shortical wants to buy AI versions of actors' faces
body: Shortical makes two-minute 'microdrama' episodes, mostly racy romances.
The first 7–10 episodes are free, then viewers pay a small monthly fee.
It's exploring AI versions of real people's faces. (TechCrunch's pick for today's venture story.)
stories.joke: Your face, now starring in its 40th episode.
stories.vc: Cheap AI content could undercut traditional TV production.

stories.headline: Stratechery's week: obituaries, agents and the iPhone Duo
body: Ben Thompson's weekly round-up gathers his writing from the week of November 16.
It covers his 'obituaries' piece on Jensen Huang and US exceptionalism.
It also includes debates about AI agents and his iPhone Duo review.
stories.joke: A week of tech, in one cup of coffee.
stories.vc: His agent analysis matters for anyone betting on AI shopping.

stories.headline: Signal limits screenshots to fight AI 'surveillance'
body: Signal is restricting screenshots in its secure messaging app.
President Meredith Whittaker says AI agents built into operating systems can scan users' screens.
She calls it an 'existential threat' to privacy. (No checkable Economist piece, so this is TechCrunch's report.)
stories.joke: Can't screenshot this headline? Blame the robots.
stories.vc: Privacy apps vs. AI agents is a new battleground for Big Tech.

stories.headline: UN Women: Afghan women are losing access to healthcare
body: UN Women says Afghanistan's rulers have issued over 100 decrees stripping women and girls of rights since 2021.
With women barred from medical training, fewer women can treat women.
That puts care for 22 million women and girls at risk.
stories.vc: UN Women gives displaced Afghan women cash aid and business training.

stories.headline: Former UN Women chief Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka dies
body: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, who led UN Women from 2013 to 2021, has died.
She was South Africa's first woman Deputy President.
She began as a teacher and anti-apartheid activist.
stories.vc: She championed women's rights and empowerment worldwide.

stories.headline: Melissa Hinmon wins lifetime award at Leaders in Trading
body: Melissa Hinmon won the Lifetime Achievement Award at The TRADE's Leaders in Trading New York 2026.
She started as a runner on the Midwest Stock Exchange floor and spent nearly four decades in markets.
She is now director of equity trading at Glenmede.
stories.joke: From running orders to running the desk.
stories.vc: Women remain rare at the top of trading desks.

stories.headline: Himachal opens a 100-bed Shahpur Civil Hospital building
body: CM Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu opened the new 100-bed Civil Hospital building in Shahpur, Kangra.
It cost ₹11.50 crore.
He said staffing in health centres has risen to nearly 70%.
stories.joke: A hundred new beds, zero waiting for paint to dry.
stories.vc: More local beds cut long trips to big-city hospitals.

stories.headline: Nanded gets a new 100-bed sub-district hospital
body: Maharashtra Deputy CM Sunetra Pawar opened a 100-bed sub-district hospital in Nanded on Friday.
She also opened a sub-divisional office and a renovated garden.
The hospital adds public beds for the district.
stories.vc: Sub-district hospitals ease pressure on overcrowded district centres.

stories.headline: Delhi-NCR becomes India's hub for robotic heart surgery
body: Delhi-NCR had 21 robotic cardiac surgery systems and about 1,800 such operations in 2025, experts say.
Numbers are expected to rise about 40% in 2026.
Both private and government hospitals are adopting it.
stories.joke: Steady robot hands for delicate hearts.
stories.vc: Hospitals are investing heavily in robots to win high-value cases.

stories.headline: Quantitative Brokers wins best execution algorithm award
body: Quantitative Brokers won the award for innovation in execution algorithms at Leaders in Trading New York 2026.
Nasdaq, Trumid and MIAX won best trading venues.
More than 150 industry leaders attended.
stories.joke: The Oscars, but for order routing.
stories.vc: Better execution algorithms mean lower trading costs for big investors.

stories.headline: Citadel names Hugh Lindsey head of electronic execution for quant team
body: Citadel has promoted Hugh Lindsey to head of electronic execution for its equity quantitative research team.
He joined in 2021 as a quantitative trader.
He most recently served as chief operating officer of the team's alpha offering.
stories.vc: Execution skill is a key edge for big quant trading firms.

stories.headline: Explainer: Why do traders cut big orders into tiny pieces?
body: Imagine buying 500 sweets from a small school shop all at once. The shopkeeper would run out and raise the price.
So you buy a few at a time, through the day, and pay less.
Big investors do the same with shares, using computer programs called execution algorithms.
This week Quantitative Brokers won an award for one of these programs.
Done well, it saves investors money; done badly, everyone sees you coming.
stories.vc: Smart slicing lowers costs for funds that hold people's savings.

stories.headline: Verstappen starts on pole in Vegas despite Antonelli's fastest lap
body: Kimi Antonelli was fastest in Las Vegas qualifying, 0.258 seconds clear of Max Verstappen.
But a five-place penalty for a new engine hands Verstappen pole.
Both Ferraris, of Leclerc and Hamilton, missed the top-10 shootout.
stories.joke: Fastest isn't always first. Ask the rulebook.
stories.vc: Engine penalties shape the show, and the TV drama, in Vegas.
